title: The 12-inch pizza deal
hook: A 12-inch pizza is twice as wide as a 6-inch one. Is it twice as much pizza?

knows: area as the number of tiles that cover a shape
a pizza's size in inches is its width (diameter)
doesNotKnow: that area scales with the square of length
the area formula for a circle (not needed)

misconception: Doubling every length of a shape doubles its area.
objective: The learner can explain that scaling every length by k multiplies area by k x k, because the shape grows in two directions at once: a 12-inch pizza has 4 times the area of a 6-inch one.

claims.text: A 12-inch round pizza has the same area as four 6-inch round pizzas.
claims.source: pi x 6^2 / (pi x 3^2) = 36 / 9 = 4. Recomputed with node.

claims.text: A box twice as wide and twice as tall holds 2 x 2 = 4 of the smaller boxes; k times as wide and tall holds k x k.
claims.source: A k-by-k square is tiled by k^2 unit squares (k rows of k).

claims.text: A circle fills the same share of the square around it at any size, so six-inch pizzas in the grid leave the same corners empty as the big one.
claims.source: Circle area pi r^2 over square area (2r)^2 is pi / 4 for every r. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): pi r^2 / (2r)^2 = pi/4 for all r.

claims.text: Scaling every length by k multiplies the area by k^2: 3 times as wide is 9 times the area, 4 times is 16.
claims.source: Area of similar plane figures scales with the square of the linear ratio (dilation by k multiplies every small square's area by k^2). Euclid, Elements VI.19-20 for similar triangles and polygons; XII.2 for circles. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Dilation by k scales area by k^2 (Euclid VI.19-20, XII.2): 3 -> 9, 4 -> 16.

recall.question: A photo is enlarged to 3 times its width and 3 times its height. How much more paper does it cover?
recall.why: Area grows in both directions at once: 3 x 3 = 9 copies of the original fit inside the enlargement.
